I'm going to try and answer some of your questions as best I can. Keep in mind that these are my ideas, not the ideas of any movement or anything.

1) I am a third-generation feminist. My grandmother received a four year college degree in the early 50s and then worked for the next 30 years. My mother was a member of NOW during the ERA era of the 70s, has held executive positions at fortune 500 tech firms, and hosts a weekly radio show about women in government. I was raised in a house where my mother made more money than my father, and my father did more of the cleaning than my mother (he learned how to clean a house when his mother died when he was 12). Both have usually had jobs, and both are respected in their fields (so much so that I'm typing very carefully so that my identity isn't discernible from this). I grew up doing woodworking with my grandfather, learning how to wire circuits and program from my father, and other not-traditionally-female things.

Now, at this point you might be thinking, "that's great! feminism did its job, and now we don't have a problem with gender. Clearly we don't, or your upbringing wouldn't have happened." Which, honestly, is mostly true. I don't really feel like I need more feminism or equality for myself. I'm much more concerned with making sure other women (and I'm talking globally), have the same right to self-determination as I did. I feel passionate about this because of how much work my forebears had to do to give me the opportunities that I have, and I certainly don't want a backslide.

That is the root of my social feminism. I want women in developing nations to be educated. I want every woman to have access to birth control. And I want real domestic (US) victims of patriarchal structures (see: the Quiverfull movement) to get out and get help.

2) My views on academic feminism are a little different. Because men were the only voices in the academic dialogue for so long (there's a part of one of William James's essays from the late 19th century where he describes women basically as another species... wish I could find it to cite), there are some basic assumptions and structures that come from a male view of the world. Now, I'm not saying that taking a feminist viewpoint would be better, just that it should be explored. I think the SEP does a decent job of describing this type of academic feminism, so linky.

3) I have a LOT of issues with the popular "feminist" movement in the United States. Why, when so many popular "feminist" websites exist, is there not one news site dedicated to serious discussions of feminism? Why would a site like Jezebel call itself feminist, then devote so much time to Ryan Gosling's abs and Kim Kardashian? Why do many tumblr users act like perma-victims, who grew up in some 19th Century hellhole where they're constantly being raped and attacked? Why do fat women try to lump that in with feminism?

And so on, and so forth.

So, here is what I believe. I believe that women are strong. I believe that although we do not have the same bodies as men, we should be able to do anything men do (as long as we pass the standards). I believe that sexually objectifying one sex without objectifying the other is indicative of a societal problem. I believe that all people should have the (UN-sponsored) rights to education and self-determination, and I believe that for women, the option of birth control (in all forms) is essential to realizing self-determination.

Please, ask me anything. I promise that my answers will be civil, even if I cannot fully answer all your questions.
